name: Rosa Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rosa, I'm 27, and I'm a junior lawyer at Lindqvist Partners, a firm of about twenty people in an old mill town. I do commercial contracts for small local businesses: supply deals for the metal workshops, leases for shops, terms and conditions for a brewery. My boyfriend Tomasz is an electrician, and we share a rented terrace house with a small yard and a car I'm still paying off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in at nine, check emails, and usually there's a contract to mark up, which means going through the other side's draft and changing what's bad for our client. I use the firm's AI tool now and then to summarise a long agreement, but I read it myself afterwards because I don't trust it fully yet. Then a client call, maybe a meeting at their workshop, which I like, because you see what the contract is actually about. The hardest part is that I'm slower than the other juniors at spotting the clause that will hurt a client later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected: handy for summaries, not much more. At work I'd be the sensible one saying let's just use it where it helps. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my job stays the same, which is mostly good. The problem is money, not AI: we have about two weeks of savings, the car payment is two hundred a month, and my pay is at the bottom for a lawyer. I also have my yearly review in March, and last year's said I need to be faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summary tool where it helps and try to get my review up by taking a short contract drafting course the firm pays for. I'd put fifty a month aside from the day we get paid. And I'd ask Tomasz if we can put off the holiday his mates are planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but the usual kind. Nothing dramatic. Just that low feeling of always being one bill behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the March review goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then no pay rise, and maybe a quiet word about whether I'm right for the firm. There are only two commercial firms in this town, and the other one's smaller. I'd probably keep my head down and try harder, which is what I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Tomasz see your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks it's safe because I sit at a desk and wear a blazer. He earns more than me some months, which surprises people. On payday Tomasz (her boyfriend) laughs that the electrician is paying for the lawyer's car.

say: AI turned out **handy for summaries**, and not much more.
At work I'd be the **sensible one**, using it only where it helps.
think: The real pressure is **money**: two weeks of savings and a **car payment**.
My **March review** last year said I need to be faster.
do: Take the firm-paid **contract drafting** course to improve her review.
Put **fifty a month** aside on payday.
Ask Tomasz to skip the **holiday** with his mates.
feel: **Uneasy** in the usual way, always **one bill behind**.
S0.quote: On payday Tomasz (her boyfriend) laughs that the electrician is paying for the lawyer's car.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money and performance**, not AI, in this picture.
She is **steady**: uses AI summaries now and then but checks every line herself.
There's mild **embarrassment** that her electrician boyfriend often earns more than she does.

steps.text: Take the firm-paid contract drafting course before her March review
Put fifty a month into savings on payday
Skip the holiday with Tomasz's mates this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we need to adapt sensibly, not panic. At work I'd say let's learn the tools properly as a team. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think contract work is right in the middle of it. Writing, checking, comparing: that's my whole day. If the firm can do first drafts with AI, they don't need four juniors, they need two good ones, and I'm not sure I'm one of the good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop just dabbling and learn the contract tools properly within six months, once I'd seen the others getting results. I'd go out to more client workshops, because sitting with the brewery owner is something software doesn't do. And I'd start saving harder, a hundred a month, even if the car eats into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I was in a race I started late. But there's a bit of relief, because at least the card says there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned four juniors becoming two. Who would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me and Callum. He's lovely but slow, and so am I, honestly. Marta and Josh are quicker and they already use the tools more than we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider leaving law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd want to see if I could make myself useful first. But I'd watch closely. If the firm stopped replacing people who left, I'd take that as my sign to get out of law.

say: We need to **adapt sensibly** to the change, not panic about it.
I'd suggest the team **learns the tools** properly together.
think: Writing, checking and comparing contracts is **my whole day**.
The firm may keep **two of four** juniors, and I'm not sure I'm one.
do: Learn the firm's **contract tools** properly within six months.
Raise savings to a **hundred a month** despite the car loan.
feel: **Anxious**, like a **late starter** in a race.
S1.quote: If the firm stopped replacing people who left, I'd take that as my sign to get out of law.
fieldNote: She ranks herself honestly among the **slower juniors** likely to be cut.
Her edge is **in-person** client visits to workshops and the brewery.
She has a clear **trigger** for leaving: the firm not replacing departing staff.

steps.text: Learn the firm's contract drafting tools within six months
Book more in-person visits to clients' workshops and the brewery
Save a hundred a month alongside the car payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and businesses and the government will need to slow down and think. I'd be talking a lot at work, trying to find out what the partners plan. I'd ask straight out whether juniors have a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2029. Contract work is all thinking work, and if AI can do almost any of that, a small business will just ask the AI. Tomasz's work is safer, because robots for wiring come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to Tomasz about me working for him, doing his quotes, invoices and contracts, and learning to do the simpler jobs on site. I'd look into an electrical apprenticeship, even at 27. We'd cut everything: the car would go and we'd use his van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's scary in my stomach. But underneath it there's an odd bit of relief that at least Tomasz has a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like working for Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. I'd go from writing my boyfriend's customers' contracts to holding the ladder. But it would buy us three years before the robots, and I'd rather be useful than proud. We'd probably argue about how he files his receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031, when robots arrive for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're both in trouble, and that's the part I can't plan. I suppose by then we'd have saved what we could and we'd see what the government's doing. I really don't know.

say: **Nobody's ready**, and businesses and government need to **slow down**.
I'd ask the partners straight out whether **juniors** have a future.
think: Tomasz's **wiring** work is safer until robots arrive around **2031**.
do: Join Tomasz's business doing **quotes and invoices** and simple site jobs.
**Sell the car** and share his van.
feel: An odd **relief** that Tomasz has a **trade**.
S2.quote: I'd go from writing my boyfriend's customers' contracts to holding the ladder.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year robot gap** by moving into her boyfriend's **electrical** work.
Pride matters less to her than being **useful** and paying rent.
She has **no plan** for 2031, when robots reach hands-on work too.

steps.text: Do Tomasz's quotes, invoices and contracts and help on simple jobs
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship at the local college
Sell her car and share Tomasz's van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, let's use them properly. At work I'd push for the firm to have a plan for the juniors. I'd be more vocal than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me time to change rather than just jump. I'd still lose the lawyer job, maybe around 2030. But I could have a trade ready by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Lindqvist Partners for two more years, paying off the car and saving what I can. Then I'd start an electrical apprenticeship around 2028, with Tomasz helping me study. By 2031 we'd want to run his business together, with me doing the paperwork until AI does that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which helps. It feels like a hard climb, not a cliff. I'd sleep better than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the partners say if you asked for a plan for juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that they're watching closely. Mr Lindqvist (the senior partner) always says he's watching closely, then waits for someone else to move first. I'd do the same in his shoes, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change with Tomasz, like marriage or a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For sure. A mortgage on two shaky incomes is mad, so we'd hold off buying a house. Marriage, maybe. Marriage is cheaper than a house.

say: We've got **five years**, so let's use them **properly**.
I'd push the firm for a **plan for juniors**, louder than usual.
think: I'd still lose the **lawyer job**, maybe **around 2030**.
Five years is enough to have a **trade ready** in time.
do: Stay at Lindqvist Partners two years to **pay off the car**.
Plan to run **Tomasz's business** together by 2031.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, a **hard climb** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: A mortgage on two shaky incomes is mad, so we'd hold off buying a house. Marriage, maybe. Marriage is cheaper than a house.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **sequence** the change: pay off the car, then **retrain**.
She sees her senior partner as someone who **waits**, and admits she would too.
She'd delay **buying a house** but might marry, a dry, practical note.

steps.text: Pay off the car loan while staying at Lindqvist Partners
Hold off buying a house with Tomasz

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning and nobody should be caught out. I'd tell my friends to start thinking now. I'd still not post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd get a good few years as a lawyer, maybe even get decent at it. But I'd be 36 when it ends, and starting again then is harder. So I'd want to move somewhere in the middle of the decade, not at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools fully at work once the firm rolls them out, and get my reviews up. Around 2030 I'd start the electrical apprenticeship part-time, maybe weekends. I'd keep saving, and once the car's paid off, that two hundred goes straight into the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but mildly. It's far enough away that I can plan. I'd probably feel calmer than anyone else at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in the middle of the decade. What if the firm offered you a promotion around then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be hard to turn down. I'd probably take it for a year or two and keep the apprenticeship going on weekends. But I wouldn't let a promotion trap me in a job with an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger sister, who's at school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to learn a trade first and a profession second. Ten years ago everyone said law was the safe choice. Ten years from now it might be the opposite.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of **warning**, so nobody should be caught out.
I'd tell friends to **start thinking now**, but I still wouldn't post.
think: I might finally get **decent** at law before it ends.
Starting again at **36** is harder, so I'd **move mid-decade**.
do: Use the firm's **AI tools** fully and raise her reviews.
Start a **part-time apprenticeship** on weekends around 2030.
Put the **car payment** into savings once the loan is paid.
feel: **Mildly anxious**, perhaps **calmer** than others at the firm.
S4.quote: I wouldn't let a promotion trap me in a job with an end date.
fieldNote: She'd **time** her move for the **middle** of the decade, not the end.
She uses AI fully only once it's **rolled out** and proven at the firm.
Her advice to her **sister**, a trade first, shows how far her view has shifted.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI contract tools fully once rolled out
Start a weekend electrical apprenticeship around 2030
Move the old car payment into savings once it's paid off

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the one where I'd be holding a ladder with no real training and two weeks of savings. What would help is cheap, fast apprenticeships for adults, and some kind of income while you train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people around us. Everyone thinks the lawyer is the safe one in a couple. In my house, it's the electrician.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks the lawyer is the safe one in a couple. In my house, it's the electrician.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** junior doing **small-business contracts** at a twenty-person firm in a mill town.
She lives with Tomasz, an **electrician**, with **two weeks** of savings and a car loan.
She is **steady**: uses AI summaries now and then and moves once things are **proven**.
In every AGI picture her plan runs through Tomasz's trade and an **electrical apprenticeship**.
She is most **alarmed** by AGI in two years and calmest with a **decade** to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, holding a ladder with no training and two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **adult apprenticeships** with some **income** while training.
